claim: DKK3 colocalizes to amyloid plaques in AD patients.
source: Studies reveal that the secreted Wnt antagonist Dickkopf-3 (DKK3) colocalizes to amyloid plaques in AD patients.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding in the abstract, citing previous studies.

claim: DKK3 expression is upregulated in the brains of AD subjects.
source: Our findings show that DKK3 expression is upregulated in the brains of AD subjects and that DKK3 protein levels increase at early stages in the disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analyses and protein measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: DKK3 protein levels increase at early stages in AD.
source: Our findings show that DKK3 expression is upregulated in the brains of AD subjects and that DKK3 protein levels increase at early stages in the disease.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from Braak I-III patients and asymptomatic AD cases showing increased DKK3 protein levels.

claim: Extracellular DKK3 levels are increased in hAPP-J20 and hAPPNL-G-F/NL-G-F mouse AD models.
source: In hAPP-J20 and hAPPNL-G-F/NL-G-F mouse AD models, extracellular DKK3 levels are increased and DKK3 accumulates at dystrophic neuronal processes around plaques.
evidence: The manuscript presents western blot data showing increased extracellular DKK3 in brain slices from these mouse models.

claim: DKK3 accumulates at dystrophic neuronal processes around plaques in AD mouse models.
source: In hAPP-J20 and hAPPNL-G-F/NL-G-F mouse AD models, extracellular DKK3 levels are increased and DKK3 accumulates at dystrophic neuronal processes around plaques.
evidence: Confocal microscopy images show DKK3 colocalization with markers of dystrophic neurites around plaques.

claim: DKK3 triggers the loss of excitatory synapses through blockade of the Wnt/GSK3β signaling.
source: Functionally, DKK3 triggers the loss of excitatory synapses through blockade of the Wnt/GSK3β signaling with a concomitant increase in inhibitory synapses via activation of the Wnt/JNK pathway.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that GSK3 inhibitors block DKK3-induced excitatory synapse loss.

claim: DKK3 increases inhibitory synapses via activation of the Wnt/JNK pathway.
source: Functionally, DKK3 triggers the loss of excitatory synapses through blockade of the Wnt/GSK3β signaling with a concomitant increase in inhibitory synapses via activation of the Wnt/JNK pathway.
evidence: The manuscript shows that JNK inhibition blocks DKK3-induced increase in inhibitory synapses.

claim: DKK3 knockdown restores synapse number in hAPP-J20 mice.
source: In contrast, DKK3 knockdown restores synapse number and memory in hAPP-J20 mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy and electrophysiology data showing restoration of synapse number after DKK3 knockdown.

claim: DKK3 knockdown restores memory in hAPP-J20 mice.
source: In contrast, DKK3 knockdown restores synapse number and memory in hAPP-J20 mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral test data showing improved memory performance after DKK3 knockdown.

claim: Synapse loss is the strongest correlate with cognitive decline in AD.
source: The disease is characterized by progressive synaptic dysfunction and loss, early signatures that correlate with cognitive decline in AD and precede both neuronal death and the onset of severe dementia by at least 10 years (Mucke and Selkoe, 2012; Selkoe and Hardy, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Synaptic dysfunction and loss precede neuronal death and the onset of severe dementia by at least 10 years in AD.
source: The disease is characterized by progressive synaptic dysfunction and loss, early signatures that correlate with cognitive decline in AD and precede both neuronal death and the onset of severe dementia by at least 10 years (Mucke and Selkoe, 2012; Selkoe and Hardy, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Soluble Aβ oligomers are considered one of the key toxic proteins driving synapse dysfunction in AD.
source: Although the primary neuropathological hallmarks of AD are amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, soluble Aβ oligomers (Aβo) are considered one of the key toxic proteins driving synapse dysfunction (Mucke and Selkoe, 2012; Selkoe and Hardy, 2016; Walsh et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Wnt signaling is compromised in AD, contributing to synapse degeneration.
source: Increasing evidence suggests that Wnt signaling is compromised in AD, contributing to synapse degeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Wnts play a crucial role in synapse formation, synaptic plasticity, and synapse integrity.
source: Wnts are secreted proteins that play a crucial role in synapse formation, synaptic plasticity, and synapse integrity (McLeod and Salinas, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The canonical Wnt pathway is particularly impaired in AD.
source: The canonical Wnt pathway is particularly impaired in AD.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple examples and citations provided in the manuscript.

claim: Levels of the secreted Wnt antagonist Dickkopf-1 (DKK1) are increased in the brain of AD patients and AD models.
source: For example, levels of the secreted Wnt antagonist Dickkopf-1 (DKK1) are increased in the brain of AD patients and AD models (Caricasole et al., 2004; Purro et al., 2012; Rosi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DKK1 promotes synapse degeneration.
source: DKK1 promotes synapse degeneration and its blockade protects against Aβ-induced dendritic spine and synapse loss (Marzo et al., 2016; Purro et al., 2012; Sellers et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Blockade of DKK1 protects against Aβ-induced dendritic spine and synapse loss.
source: DKK1 promotes synapse degeneration and its blockade protects against Aβ-induced dendritic spine and synapse loss (Marzo et al., 2016; Purro et al., 2012; Sellers et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Three genetic variants of LRP6 are linked to late-onset AD and confer decreased Wnt signaling in cell lines.
source: Supporting the role of deficient Wnt signaling in AD, three genetic variants of LRP6, a crucial Wnt co-receptor, are linked to late-onset AD and confer decreased Wnt signaling in cell lines (Alarcón et al., 2013; De Ferrari et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mice carrying the Lrp6-Valine variant exhibit increased synapse vulnerability during aging and in AD.
source: Notably, mice carrying the Lrp6-Valine variant exhibit increased synapse vulnerability during aging and in AD (Jones et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Loss-of-function of Lrp6 exacerbates amyloid pathology in an AD mouse model.
source: Furthermore, loss-of-function of Lrp6 exacerbates amyloid pathology in an AD mouse model (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Frizzled-1 (Fz1) and Fz7 are downregulated in the hippocampus of AD subjects and AD models.
source: In addition, Frizzled-1 (Fz1) and Fz7, Wnt receptors present at synapses, are downregulated in the hippocampus of AD subjects and AD models (Palomer et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: DKK3 is increased in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in human AD.
source: Recent findings indicate that DKK3 is increased in plasma, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and accumulates in Aβ plaques in the human AD brain (Bruggink et al., 2015; Drummond et al., 2017; Xiong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DKK3 accumulates in Aβ plaques in the human AD brain.
source: Recent findings indicate that DKK3 is increased in plasma, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and accumulates in Aβ plaques in the human AD brain (Bruggink et al., 2015; Drummond et al., 2017; Xiong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DKK3 expression is increased in AD cases based on logistic regression analyses of RNAseq data.
source: Logistic regression analyses revealed that DKK3 was upregulated in AD cases (regression β-coefficient=0.31; p-value = 1.52 × 10–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of RNAseq data from multiple datasets.

claim: DKK3 is differentially expressed in relation to Braak scores.
source: In addition, ordinal regression analyses showed that DKK3 was differentially expressed in relation to Braak scores, a measure of neurofibrillary tangle pathology (Braak et al., 2006; regression β-coefficient=0.27; p-value = 8.84 × 10–4), but not to CERAD scores, a measure of neuritic plaque density (Mirra et al., 1991; regression β-coefficient: 0.07; p-value = 0.43; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of RNAseq data and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DKK3 is not differentially expressed in relation to CERAD scores.
source: In addition, ordinal regression analyses showed that DKK3 was differentially expressed in relation to Braak scores, a measure of neurofibrillary tangle pathology (Braak et al., 2006; regression β-coefficient=0.27; p-value = 8.84 × 10–4), but not to CERAD scores, a measure of neuritic plaque density (Mirra et al., 1991; regression β-coefficient: 0.07; p-value = 0.43; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of RNAseq data and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Soluble DKK3 levels are increased in Braak I-III patients compared to control subjects.
source: Soluble DKK3 levels were increased in Braak I-III patients when compared to control subjects (1.4-fold increase), but no changes were observed in Braak IV-VI (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No changes in soluble DKK3 levels were observed in Braak IV-VI patients compared to controls.
source: Soluble DKK3 levels were increased in Braak I-III patients when compared to control subjects (1.4-fold increase), but no changes were observed in Braak IV-VI (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DKK3 protein levels in the insoluble fraction are increased in Braak IV-VI patients.
source: In the insoluble fraction, in contrast, DKK3 protein levels were increased in Braak IV-Vl (1.51-fold increase; Figure 1C), which could be consistent with the presence of DKK3 in Aβ plaques.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DKK3 protein is elevated in AD cases based on proteomic analysis.
source: In line with our above results, DKK3 protein was elevated in AD cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of a published proteomic dataset.

claim: DKK3 is increased in asymptomatic AD cases.
source: Importantly, DKK3 was increased in asymptomatic AD cases and further increased in AD cases when compared to asymptomatic AD (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: DKK3 is further increased in AD cases when compared to asymptomatic AD.
source: Importantly, DKK3 was increased in asymptomatic AD cases and further increased in AD cases when compared to asymptomatic AD (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: DKK3 protein is re-distributed from soluble to insoluble fractions with AD disease progression.
source: Moreover, DKK3 protein is re-distributed from soluble to insoluble fractions with disease progression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing increased soluble DKK3 in early stages and increased insoluble DKK3 in later stages.

claim: Dkk3 is expressed in excitatory neurons in the hippocampus and neocortex.
source: Dkk3 is expressed in excitatory neurons in several brain areas including the hippocampus and neocortex (Barrantes et al., 2006; Meister et al., 2015; Thompson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DKK3 protein is highly abundant in neurons of the CA1, CA2, and CA3 pyramidal layers but not in the dentate gyrus (DG) granule cell layer.
source: In the hippocampus, DKK3 protein was highly abundant in neurons of the CA1, CA2, and CA3 pyramidal layers but not in the dentate gyrus (DG) granule cell layer (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), consistent with previous works studying Dkk3 expression (Barrantes et al., 2006; Thompson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DKK3 protein is present at lower levels in a subset of astrocytes.
source: In addition, DKK3 protein was present at lower levels in a subset of astrocytes (GFAP-positive cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), but not in microglia (IBA1-positive cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: DKK3 protein is not present in microglia.
source: In addition, DKK3 protein was present at lower levels in a subset of astrocytes (GFAP-positive cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), but not in microglia (IBA1-positive cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Principal neurons, followed by astrocytes, are the main source of DKK3 protein in the adult mouse hippocampus.
source: Thus, principal neurons, followed by astrocytes, are the main source of DKK3 protein in the adult mouse hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing DKK3 expression patterns in different cell types.

claim: DKK3 is present at Aβ plaques in 18-month-old J20 and 8-month-old hAPPNL-G-F/NL-G-F mice.
source: Using confocal microscopy, we investigated the presence of DKK3 in hippocampal Aβ plaques using anti-Aβ (6E10) in 18-month-old J20 (Mucke et al., 2000a) and 8-month-old hAPPNL-G-F/NL-G-F (NLGF) mice (Saito et al., 2014). DKK3 was present at Aβ plaques in both AD lines (Figure 2B andFigure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: DKK3 is present in both diffuse Aβ plaques and dense-core plaques.
source: Furthermore, DKK3 was present in both diffuse Aβ plaques (6E10-positive but ThioS negative) and dense-core plaques (positive for 6E10 and ThioS; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 70% of dense-core Aβ plaques contain DKK3.
source: Importantly, 70% of dense-core Aβ plaques contained DKK3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Wnt7a/b does not localize to Aβ plaques.
source: This localization was specific for DKK3, as other secreted proteins such as Wnt7a/b did not localize to Aβ plaques (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: DKK3 is absent from astrocytes and microglia in Aβ plaques.
source: Furthermore, DKK3 was absent from astrocytes and microglia in Aβ plaques but specifically colocalized with Neurofilament-H +dystrophic neurites (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: DKK3 specifically colocalizes with Neurofilament-H positive dystrophic neurites.
source: Furthermore, DKK3 was absent from astrocytes and microglia in Aβ plaques but specifically colocalized with Neurofilament-H +dystrophic neurites (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy images and Pearson's correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DKK3 colocalizes with LAMP1 in dystrophic neurites.
source: In addition, DKK3 also colocalized with LAMP1 in dystrophic neurites, which are visualized as axonal spheroids (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy images and Pearson's correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Total DKK3 levels do not differ between J20 and WT mice in brain homogenates at 3-4 months.
source: Although the total DKK3 levels did not differ between J20 and WT mice in the brain homogenate, DKK3 levels were significantly increased (2.54-fold) in the extracellular fraction of J20 mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: DKK3 levels are significantly increased (2.54-fold) in the extracellular fraction of J20 mice at 3-4 months.
source: Although the total DKK3 levels did not differ between J20 and WT mice in the brain homogenate, DKK3 levels were significantly increased (2.54-fold) in the extracellular fraction of J20 mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Extracellular DKK3 levels are elevated by 2.43-fold in brain slices of NLGF mice at 2-3 months.
source: In a second AD mouse model, NLGF, extracellular DKK3 levels were also elevated by 2.43-fold in brain slices of these animals at 2–3 months (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The ratio of extracellular to total DKK3 levels is significantly higher in J20 and NLGF compared to their respective controls.
source: Importantly, the ratio of extracellular to total DKK3 levels was significantly higher in J20 and NLGF when compared to their respective controls (Figure 2E and F), suggesting that DKK3 secretion is enhanced in AD mouse brains.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: DKK3 secretion is enhanced in AD mouse brains.
source: Importantly, the ratio of extracellular to total DKK3 levels was significantly higher in J20 and NLGF when compared to their respective controls (Figure 2E and F), suggesting that DKK3 secretion is enhanced in AD mouse brains.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing increased ratio of extracellular to total DKK3.

claim: Aβo trigger the overactivation of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors (NMDARs), which contributes to long-term depression (LTD) in AD models.
source: Mounting evidence demonstrates that Aβo trigger the overactivation of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors (NMDARs), which contributes to long-term depression (LTD) in AD models (Li et al., 2011; Mucke and Selkoe, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: APV completely prevents the increase of DKK3 in the extracellular fraction of J20 and NLGF brain slices.
source: APV completely prevented the increase of DKK3 in the extracellular fraction of J20 and NLGF brain slices (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Aβo increase DKK3 protein levels by 2.50-fold in the cellular lysate and 2.48-fold in the extracellular fraction of hippocampal neurons.
source: Aβo increased DKK3 protein levels by 2.50- and 2.48-fold in the cellular lysate and the extracellular fraction respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F–H), indicating that Aβo increased the overall levels of DKK3 in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F–H.

claim: Induction of cLTP does not affect DKK3 protein levels in the cellular or extracellular fractions.
source: Induction of cLTP did not affect DKK3 protein levels in the cellular or extracellular fractions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: cLTD significantly increases the levels of extracellular DKK3 without affecting the levels in the cellular fractions.
source: In contrast, cLTD significantly increased the levels of extracellular DKK3 without affecting the levels in the cellular fractions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: BFA treatment significantly reduces DKK3 levels in the extracellular space under control conditions.
source: We found that BFA treatment significantly reduced DKK3 levels in the extracellular space under control conditions and completely prevented the increase in DKK3 levels following cLTD-induction (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: BFA completely prevents the increase in DKK3 levels following cLTD-induction.
source: We found that BFA treatment significantly reduced DKK3 levels in the extracellular space under control conditions and completely prevented the increase in DKK3 levels following cLTD-induction (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Trafficking/secretion of DKK3 is enhanced by NMDAR-mediated cLTD-induction.
source: Together, these results strongly suggest that trafficking/secretion of DKK3 was enhanced by NMDAR-mediated cLTD-induction.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing increased extracellular DKK3 after cLTD and blockade by BFA.

claim: DKK3 gain-of-function reduces vGLUT1 puncta number by 38.99% in the CA3 SR.
source: Gain-of-function of DKK3 reduced the puncta number of the excitatory presynaptic marker vGLUT1 (by 38.99%), the postsynaptic marker PSD-95 (by 32.58%), and the total number of excitatory synapses (by 60.85%), determined by the colocalization of these synaptic markers, in the CA3 SR (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: DKK3 gain-of-function reduces PSD-95 puncta number by 32.58% in the CA3 SR.
source: Gain-of-function of DKK3 reduced the puncta number of the excitatory presynaptic marker vGLUT1 (by 38.99%), the postsynaptic marker PSD-95 (by 32.58%), and the total number of excitatory synapses (by 60.85%), determined by the colocalization of these synaptic markers, in the CA3 SR (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: DKK3 gain-of-function reduces the total number of excitatory synapses by 60.85% in the CA3 SR.
source: Gain-of-function of DKK3 reduced the puncta number of the excitatory presynaptic marker vGLUT1 (by 38.99%), the postsynaptic marker PSD-95 (by 32.58%), and the total number of excitatory synapses (by 60.85%), determined by the colocalization of these synaptic markers, in the CA3 SR (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: DKK3 gain-of-function decreases the frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSC) by 48.54%.
source: Patch-clamp recordings of CA3 neurons revealed that DKK3 gain-of-function decreased the frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSC) by 48.54% but did not affect their amplitude (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: DKK3 gain-of-function does not affect mEPSC amplitude.
source: Patch-clamp recordings of CA3 neurons revealed that DKK3 gain-of-function decreased the frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSC) by 48.54% but did not affect their amplitude (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: DKK3 increases the density of gephyrin puncta by 55.39% in the CA3 SR.
source: DKK3 increased the density of puncta for the inhibitory postsynaptic marker gephyrin (by 55.39%) without affecting the density of the inhibitory presynaptic marker vGAT in the CA3 SR (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: DKK3 does not affect the density of the inhibitory presynaptic marker vGAT in the CA3 SR.
source: DKK3 increased the density of puncta for the inhibitory postsynaptic marker gephyrin (by 55.39%) without affecting the density of the inhibitory presynaptic marker vGAT in the CA3 SR (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: DKK3 increases the number of inhibitory synapses by 65.99% in the CA3 SR.
source: Notably, DKK3 increased the number of inhibitory synapses (by 65.99%; Figure 3D) based on the colocalization of the pre and postsynaptic markers.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: DKK3 increases the frequency of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSC) by 65.56%.
source: Patch-clamp recordings of CA3 neurons uncovered that DKK3 increased the frequency of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSC) by 65.56% but did not affect their amplitude (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: DKK3 does not affect mIPSC amplitude.
source: Patch-clamp recordings of CA3 neurons uncovered that DKK3 increased the frequency of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSC) by 65.56% but did not affect their amplitude (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: DKK3 decreases the number of extra-synaptic β-catenin puncta in hippocampal slices.
source: Indeed, DKK3 decreased the number of extra-synaptic β-catenin puncta in hippocampal slices, which was restored when the Wnt/GSK3β cascade was activated using the GSK3 inhibitor 6-bromoindirubin-3'-oxime (BIO) (Marzo et al., 2016; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BIO restores the number of extra-synaptic β-catenin puncta decreased by DKK3.
source: Indeed, DKK3 decreased the number of extra-synaptic β-catenin puncta in hippocampal slices, which was restored when the Wnt/GSK3β cascade was activated using the GSK3 inhibitor 6-bromoindirubin-3'-oxime (BIO) (Marzo et al., 2016; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BIO increases the density of extra-synaptic β-catenin puncta under control conditions.
source: Importantly, BIO increased the density of extra-synaptic β-catenin puncta under control conditions, confirming the activation of canonical Wnt signaling (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BIO does not affect the number of excitatory synapses under control brain slices.
source: At the concentration and time used, BIO did not affect the number of excitatory synapses under control brain slices, but completely blocked the DKK3-induced loss of excitatory synapses (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: BIO completely blocks the DKK3-induced loss of excitatory synapses.
source: At the concentration and time used, BIO did not affect the number of excitatory synapses under control brain slices, but completely blocked the DKK3-induced loss of excitatory synapses (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CHIR99021 blocks the effect of DKK3 on excitatory synapses.
source: Similar results were obtained with CHIR99021, another highly specific GSK3 inhibitor (Ring et al., 2003; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DKK3 affects excitatory synapse number through the Wnt/GSK3β pathway.
source: Thus, DKK3 affects excitatory synapse number through the Wnt/GSK3β pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that GSK3 inhibitors block DKK3-induced excitatory synapse loss.

claim: BIO does not affect DKK3's impact on inhibitory synapse density.
source: In contrast to excitatory synapses, BIO did not affect DKK3's impact on inhibitory synapse density (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DKK3 increases phospho-JNK in brain slices.
source: In brain slices, DKK3 increased phospho-JNK, a readout for the JNK activation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CC-930 blocks the DKK3-induced increase in phospho-JNK.
source: This increase was blocked by the JNK inhibitor CC-930 (Plantevin Krenitsky et al., 2012; Figure 4E), indicating that DKK3 activates the Wnt/JNK signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: DKK3 activates the Wnt/JNK signaling pathway.
source: This increase was blocked by the JNK inhibitor CC-930 (Plantevin Krenitsky et al., 2012; Figure 4E), indicating that DKK3 activates the Wnt/JNK signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that DKK3 increases phospho-JNK and this is blocked by a JNK inhibitor.

claim: CC-930 blocks the DKK3-induced increase in the number of gephyrin puncta and inhibitory synapse density.
source: We next tested the effect of CC-930 on inhibitory synapses and found that this JNK inhibitor blocked the DKK3-induced increase in the number of gephyrin puncta and inhibitory synapse density (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: JNK inhibition does not block the effect of DKK3 on excitatory synapses.
source: In contrast, JNK inhibition did not block the effect of DKK3 on excitatory synapses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DKK3 induces the loss of excitatory synapses through inhibition of Wnt/GSK3β signaling.
source: Together, our results indicate that DKK3 induces the loss of excitatory synapses through inhibition of Wnt/GSK3β signaling but increases inhibitory synapses through activation of the Wnt/JNK pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that GSK3 inhibitors block DKK3-induced excitatory synapse loss.

claim: DKK3 increases inhibitory synapses through activation of the Wnt/JNK pathway.
source: Together, our results indicate that DKK3 induces the loss of excitatory synapses through inhibition of Wnt/GSK3β signaling but increases inhibitory synapses through activation of the Wnt/JNK pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that JNK inhibition blocks DKK3-induced inhibitory synapse increase.

claim: DKK3 silencing does not affect excitatory synapse number in WT mice.
source: In contrast to gain-of-function experiments, DKK3 silencing did not affect excitatory synapse number (Figure 5B) or mEPSC frequency (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy and electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: DKK3 silencing does not affect mEPSC frequency in WT mice.
source: In contrast to gain-of-function experiments, DKK3 silencing did not affect excitatory synapse number (Figure 5B) or mEPSC frequency (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DKK3 loss-of-function decreases the amplitude of mEPSCs by 28.18% in WT mice.
source: However, DKK3 loss-of-function decreased the amplitude of mEPSCs (by 28.18%, Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of DKK3 reduces the number of inhibitory synapses by 37.30% in WT mice.
source: Conversely, knockdown of DKK3 reduced the number of inhibitory synapses (by 37.30%, Figure 5D), the frequency of mIPSCs (by 71.76%), and their amplitude (by 35.02%, Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Knockdown of DKK3 reduces the frequency of mIPSCs by 71.76% in WT mice.
source: Conversely, knockdown of DKK3 reduced the number of inhibitory synapses (by 37.30%, Figure 5D), the frequency of mIPSCs (by 71.76%), and their amplitude (by 35.02%, Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Knockdown of DKK3 reduces the amplitude of mIPSCs by 35.02% in WT mice.
source: Conversely, knockdown of DKK3 reduced the number of inhibitory synapses (by 37.30%, Figure 5D), the frequency of mIPSCs (by 71.76%), and their amplitude (by 35.02%, Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Endogenous DKK3 is required for the maintenance of inhibitory synapses but not for the integrity of excitatory synapses in the healthy adult brain.
source: Thus, downregulation of DKK3 in WT brain reduces the number of inhibitory synapses without affecting excitatory synapses, suggesting that endogenous DKK3 is required for the maintenance of inhibitory synapses but not for the integrity of excitatory synapses in the healthy adult brain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing differential effects of DKK3 knockdown on excitatory and inhibitory synapses.

claim: 4-month-old J20 mice exhibit a 40-45% loss of excitatory synapses in the CA3 SR compared to WT.
source: We found that 4-month-old J20 mice exhibited a 40–45% loss of excitatory synapses in the CA3 SR when compared to WT (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) as previously reported (Hong et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: DKK3 knockdown restores excitatory synapse number in 4-month-old J20 mice.
source: Remarkably, DKK3 knockdown restored excitatory synapse number in J20 mice (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibitory synapses are increased by 20.60% in 4-month-old J20 mice compared to WT.
source: In contrast to excitatory synapses, inhibitory synapses were increased by 20.60% in J20 mice compared to WT (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DKK3 silencing decreases inhibitory synapse number in 4-month-old J20 mice.
source: Importantly, DKK3 silencing decreased inhibitory synapse number in these mice (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In vivo DKK3 loss-of-function ameliorates synaptic defects in J20 mice.
source: Thus, in vivo DKK3 loss-of-function ameliorates synaptic defects in J20 mice, supporting the hypothesis that DKK3 is a key contributor to synaptic changes in this AD mouse model.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing restoration of synapse number after DKK3 knockdown in J20 mice.

claim: DKK3 silencing significantly increases the number of excitatory synapses around plaques in 9-month-old J20 mice.
source: Importantly, DKK3 silencing significantly increased the number of excitatory synapses (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) but decreased the density of inhibitory synapses around plaques (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) when compared to J20 mice injected with Scr shRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: DKK3 silencing decreases the density of inhibitory synapses around plaques in 9-month-old J20 mice.
source: Importantly, DKK3 silencing significantly increased the number of excitatory synapses (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) but decreased the density of inhibitory synapses around plaques (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) when compared to J20 mice injected with Scr shRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Knockdown of DKK3 does not affect the number or size of plaques in the CA3 SR.
source: Importantly, knockdown of DKK3 did not affect the number or size of plaques in the CA3 SR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Modulation of DKK3 levels does not affect Dkk1 mRNA levels in the hippocampus of WT and J20 mice.
source: Given the role of DKK1 in synaptic changes and in AD (Caricasole et al., 2004; Marzo et al., 2016; Purro et al., 2012), we next investigated whether modulation of DKK3 levels affected Dkk1 mRNA levels in the hippocampus of WT and J20 mice injected with Scr or Dkk3 shRNA. However, no changes in Dkk1 mRNA levels were observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Increased Dkk1 does not lead to changes in Dkk3 expression.
source: We next investigated whether increased Dkk1 led to changes in Dkk3 expression. For this, we used a transgenic mouse model that expresses Dkk1 upon induction (iDkk1 mice; Galli et al., 2021; Galli et al., 2014; Marzo et al., 2016). After 14 days of Dkk1 expression and when synaptic changes are observed in these mice, we found that Dkk3 levels were unaltered in the hippocampus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Dkk3's expression is unaffected by Dkk1 and vice versa.
source: Thus, Dkk3's expression is unaffected by Dkk1 and vice versa.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing no changes in Dkk1 or Dkk3 expression when the other is modulated.

claim: Loss-of-function of DKK3 ameliorates excitatory and inhibitory synapse changes in J20 mice independently of DKK1 before plaque burden starts (4-months-old), and later when amyloid plaque pathology is evident (9-month-old).
source: Together, these results demonstrate that loss-of-function of DKK3 ameliorates excitatory and inhibitory synapse changes in J20 mice independently of DKK1 before plaque burden starts (4-months-old), and later when amyloid plaque pathology is evident (9-month-old).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing restoration of synapse number after DKK3 knockdown at different disease stages and the lack of effect on Dkk1 expression.

claim: Knockdown of DKK3 using viral injections does not affect exploratory activity or anxiety in J20 mice.
source: Knockdown of DKK3 using viral injections did not affect exploratory activity or anxiety in J20 mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: DKK3 downregulation significantly improves spatial memory in J20 mice as evaluated by the novel object location test (NOLT).
source: In contrast, DKK3 downregulation significantly improved spatial memory in J20 mice as evaluated by the novel object location test (NOLT) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Silencing DKK3 in J20 mice fully rescues the defect in escape latency during Morris Water Maze training.
source: Performance improved significantly in all 4 groups during training, although the escape latency in J20-Scr shRNA mice remained significantly higher than that of WT-Scr shRNA mice (Figure 7C). Importantly, silencing DKK3 in J20 mice fully rescued this defect (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In the early probe test, J20-Scr shRNA animals traveled significantly less in the target quadrant than WT-Scr shRNA mice.
source: In the first early probe test, J20-Scr shRNA animals traveled significantly less in the target quadrant than WT-Scr shRNA mice (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In the late probe, the time to first entrance to the target location and the distance traveled in the target quadrant are restored in the J20-Dkk3 shRNA mice compared to J20-Scr shRNA mice.
source: After further training, in the late probe, the time to first entrance to the target location (platform) and the distance traveled in the target quadrant were restored in the J20- Dkk3 shRNA mice when compared to J20-Scr shRNA mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: DKK3 downregulation in the hippocampus restores cognitive function in J20 AD mice.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that DKK3 downregulation in the hippocampus restores cognitive function in J20 AD mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral test data showing improved memory performance after DKK3 knockdown.

claim: DKK3 is a potential target for ameliorating excitatory and inhibitory synaptic impairment and memory dysfunction in AD.
source: Thus, DKK3 is a potential target for ameliorating excitatory and inhibitory synaptic impairment and memory dysfunction in AD.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the functional studies showing that DKK3 knockdown restores synapses and memory in AD mouse models.

claim: DKK3 is the most highly expressed member of the DKK family of Wnt antagonists in the human and mouse brain.
source: DKK3 is the most highly expressed member of the DKK family of Wnt antagonists in the human and mouse brain (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: DKK1 only affects excitatory synapses in the hippocampus.
source: These results are in contrast to those obtained with DKK1, which only affects excitatory synapses in the hippocampus (Marzo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The activity of GSK3β is increased in the AD brain, which is associated with reduced Wnt signalling.
source: The activity of GSK3β is increased in the AD brain, which is associated with reduced Wnt signalling (Leroy et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: GSK3β plays a role in the production of mitochondrial ATP, a key event in maintaining synapses.
source: GSK3β also plays a role in the production of mitochondrial ATP, a key event in maintaining synapses (Gomez-Suaga et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mitochondrial function is disrupted in the presence of toxic proteins such as Tau and recovered by inhibition of GSK3β.
source: However, this function is disrupted in the presence of toxic proteins such as Tau and, importantly, recovered by inhibition of GSK3β (Gomez-Suaga et al., 2022; Szabo et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DKK3 could contribute to the loss of excitatory synapses by impairing mitochondrial function through activation of GSK3β.
source: Thus, DKK3 could also contribute to the loss of excitatory synapses by impairing mitochondrial function through activation of GSK3β.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the known role of GSK3β in mitochondrial function.

claim: DKK3 activates JNK in the hippocampus.
source: Our finding that DKK3 activates JNK in the hippocampus is consistent with previous results in other cell types (Abarzua et al., 2005; Mizobuchi et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of synapses around amyloid plaques is well described.
source: Although loss of synapses around amyloid plaques is well described (Koffie et al., 2012), changes in synapse number induced by silencing DKK3 is unlikely to be due to the formation of plaques as we observed similar synaptic changes when plaques are absent.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Changes in synapse number induced by silencing DKK3 are unlikely to be due to the formation of plaques.
source: Although loss of synapses around amyloid plaques is well described (Koffie et al., 2012), changes in synapse number induced by silencing DKK3 is unlikely to be due to the formation of plaques as we observed similar synaptic changes when plaques are absent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing synaptic changes after DKK3 knockdown in young mice before plaque deposition.

claim: DKK3 directly affects the integrity of excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: Moreover, our gain-of-function studies demonstrate that DKK3 directly affects the integrity of excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the gain-of-function experiments showing synaptic changes after DKK3 treatment.

claim: The rescue of the synaptic and cognitive defects is specific to DKK3 downregulation.
source: The rescue of the synaptic and cognitive defects is specific to DKK3 downregulation as no differences in Dkk1 levels, a Wnt antagonist that affects synapses (Marzo et al., 2016), are observed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing no changes in Dkk1 expression after DKK3 knockdown.
